title: Ban on landlord use of coordinated pricing algorithms to set rents or occupancy

coverage_conditions: All landlords of residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.

penalty: City Attorney civil action for damages, injunctive relief, restitution and civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation. An aggrieved tenant may sue for injunctive relief, damages and civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation. Prevailing plaintiffs recover attorney's fees.

Government-owned or subsidized units (e.g., Section 8, Shelter Plus Care, VASH, LIHTC, HOME) are now fully or partially covered depending on unit type.
exemptions: Partially covered units (no rent ceiling): new construction (certificate of occupancy issued after 1980), most single-family homes, most condominiums, and certain subsidized units where federal/state law prohibits rent control (Section 202, Section 811, HUD-insured/held projects). citation: Berkeley Rent Ordinance, as amended by Measure BB (Nov. 2024)

title: Security deposit capped at first month's rent

title: Optional fee in lieu of security deposit (by regulation)

title: Security deposit must be held in separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account
requirement: Security deposits must be held in a separate, interest-bearing account in a Massachusetts bank, protected from the lessor's creditors, and the tenant must receive a receipt with the bank name, location, amount and account number within 30 days.

title: Annual interest on security deposits and last month's rent

quoted_span: A lessor of residential real property who holds a security deposit pursuant to this section for a period of one year or longer from the commencement of the term of the tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of the tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year, or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable to the tenant at the end of each year of the tenancy.

title: Deposit receipt and statement of condition
requirement: A lessor who accepts a security deposit must give a signed receipt and, within 10 days after the tenancy begins (or on receipt, if later), a written statement of the premises' condition listing existing damage, with a prescribed notice; the lessor must keep deposit records for two years.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Does not apply to vacation/recreational tenancies of 100 days or less.

quoted_span: Any lessor of residential real property, or his agent, who accepts a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall, upon receipt of such security deposit, or within ten days after commencement of the tenancy, whichever is later, furnish to such tenant or prospective tenant a separate written statement of the present condition of the premises to be leased or rented.

title: Return of security deposit within 30 days; limited deductions
requirement: The lessor must return the deposit (or balance) within 30 days after the tenancy ends, deducting only unpaid rent/water charges, qualifying tax escalation amounts, and reasonable repair costs for tenant-caused damage beyond normal wear and tear, supported by a sworn itemized list.
key_value: 30 days
coverage_conditions: All residential lessors holding a security deposit.
exemptions: Vacation or recreational leases or tenancies of 100 days or less.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Does not apply to vacation/recreational tenancies of 100 days or less.

title: Transfer of security deposit and last month's rent to successor owner
requirement: When a lessor transfers the property, the deposit (and any last month's rent advance) with accrued interest must be transferred to the successor, who must notify the tenant in writing within 45 days; a successor who does not receive the deposit is still liable for it.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Successor liability exemption depends on successor type (municipality or chartered financial institution).

title: Anti-retaliation protection for tenants (reprisal presumption)
requirement: Landlords may not threaten or take reprisals against tenants for enforcing housing laws, reporting code violations, complaining to the landlord in writing, or joining a tenants' union. A termination notice (other than for nonpayment), rent increase, or substantial change in tenancy terms within six months of such activity is presumed retaliatory unless the landlord rebuts it by clear and convincing evidence.
key_value: 6-month rebuttable presumption; damages 1-3 months' rent or actual damages, whichever greater
coverage_conditions: Tenants of residential premises in Massachusetts who engaged in protected activity, such as enforcing housing laws, reporting violations, written complaints to the landlord, or tenants' union organizing. Lease waivers are void.
exemptions: The presumption does not apply to termination notices for nonpayment of rent.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Applies only where the tenant (or someone on the tenant's behalf) engaged in protected activity within the prior six months

penalty: Damages of not less than one month's rent or more than three months' rent, or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus costs of suit and reasonable attorney's fee
quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities.

title: Limit on charges before start of tenancy (no application fees by lessors)
requirement: Before a tenancy begins, a landlord may require payment only of first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit, and a lock-change fee. Application, pet, cleaning, amenity and all other upfront charges by the lessor are forbidden.
key_value: Only first month's rent, last month's rent, security deposit, lock-change fee
coverage_conditions: All lessors of residential rental property in Massachusetts, at or before the start of a tenancy.
exemptions: Licensed real estate brokers acting as a separate bona fide business may charge fees under 254 CMR 7.00, according to the article.
penalty: Tenants have recovered treble damages and attorney's fees for unlawful application fees (Perry v. Equity Residential Management, D. Mass. 2014).
quoted_span: It states that prior to the beginning of a tenancy, no lessor may require payment for anything except first, last, security, and locks ( MGL Ch 186 Section 15B ).
conflict_note: Secondary source (landlord trade association blog). It gives the effective date only as 'since the 1970s'. The article advises that requiring applicants to pay third-party screening services is legally risky, but there is no case law on that point.

title: Licensed broker fee disclosure requirements for prospective tenants
requirement: Only licensed brokers or salespersons may charge prospective tenants a fee for finding housing. At the first personal meeting, the broker must give a written notice stating the fee amount, the time and manner of payment, and whether the fee depends on a lease being signed. The applicant signs the notice, or the broker records the refusal.
coverage_conditions: Licensed real estate brokers and salespersons who find rental housing for prospective tenants for a fee.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Applies only when a licensed broker is involved in the transaction.

quoted_span: In addition to holding a valid license, the broker has to tell the applicant in writing the amount of the broker’s fee, the time and manner of payment, and whether it is contingent on the owner and applicant actually entering into a lease or rental agreement.
conflict_note: This is an archived secondary article with no effective date given. Later Massachusetts legislation on who pays broker fees may have changed tenant-paid broker fees; this document does not reflect any such change, so verify current law.

title: Initiative Petition 25-21, 'An Initiative Petition to Protect Tenants by Limiting Rent Increases' (statewide rent control ballot initiative)
requirement: Would have repealed the statutory ban on rent control (G.L. c. 40P) and capped annual rent increases for most residential rental units at the lesser of the annual CPI increase or 5%. The SJC barred it from the November 2026 ballot, so it never took effect.
key_value: Lesser of annual CPI increase or 5%
coverage_conditions: Most residential rental units statewide in Massachusetts (as proposed).
exemptions: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units; newly constructed units less than 10 years old; certain publicly regulated units; short-term rentals; dwelling units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or nonprofit purposes.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Proposed exemptions for certain publicly regulated units, short-term rentals, and units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or nonprofit purposes; owner-occupied exemption applied only to buildings with four or fewer units.

title: Broker fee paid only by the party that hired the broker
requirement: A licensed broker or salesperson may contract with either the prospective tenant or the landlord (or landlord's agent), but not both. Any broker fee may be paid only by the party that originally hired the broker, so tenants cannot be charged a landlord-hired broker's fee.
key_value: Fee paid only by the party who engaged the broker
coverage_conditions: Rental residential real property in Massachusetts where a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is engaged to find a tenant or a rental.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Applies only where a licensed broker or salesperson is involved in the rental transaction.

title: Required state form accompanying notice to quit for nonpayment of rent
requirement: A written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent to a residential tenant must come with a state-developed form. The form must document any repayment agreement, give information on rental assistance, court rules and eviction restrictions, and state that the notice is not an eviction. title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
requirement: Residential rental property owners may not use algorithmic revenue management software that collects or processes competitors' nonpublic leasing information to set or recommend rents. requirement: A landlord or its agent may not charge an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental unit. Starting January 1, 2027, the cap is adjusted each year for CPI increases and published by the Division of Consumer Affairs.

title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act good-cause requirement
requirement: A residential landlord may not evict a tenant or refuse to renew a written or oral lease without one of the statutory good causes. The landlord must serve the required Notice to Quit, and a Notice to Cease where applicable.

requirement: A tenant evicted so the landlord can correct an illegal occupancy is entitled to relocation assistance from the landlord equal to six times the monthly rent. title: Prohibition on self-help evictions and lockouts
requirement: Landlords may not lock out tenants, change locks, shut off utilities or remove tenants without a court judgment. Only a court officer acting under a warrant for removal may physically evict a tenant.

penalty: Damages, court costs and attorney fees; treble damages where possession cannot be restored (N.J.S.A. 2A:39-8); possible disorderly conduct charge
quoted_span: Self-help evictions, or lockouts, made by the landlord are illegal in New Jersey.

title: Anti-reprisal protection for tenants
requirement: A landlord may not evict, substantially alter the lease, or refuse to renew in reprisal when a tenant does any of the following: enforces legal rights, makes a good-faith code complaint, or joins a tenant organization.

quoted_span:
A landlord cannot take reprisal action against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of

title: Foreclosure Fairness Act tenant notices and protections
requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction. Within 10 business days after a foreclosure sale, the new owner must notify tenants in English and Spanish that they are not required to move. Any cash-for-keys offer must be voluntary and accompanied by the required notice.

title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (conversions)
requirement: Eligible senior, disabled, or disabled-veteran tenants in buildings converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership may be protected from eviction for up to 40 years, subject to income limits. Converters must notify tenants of the right to apply.

requirement: Landlords must give each tenant the DCA Truth in Renting Statement within 30 days of its posting. They must also give it to each new tenant at or before lease signing.

title: Security deposit cap of 1.5 months' rent
requirement: A security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent, and that cap includes any pet deposits and prepaid rent such as last month's rent. Any annual increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit.

title: Security deposit holding, interest and notice requirements
requirement: Deposits must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account at a New Jersey institution, with interest belonging to the tenant and paid annually. The landlord must give written notice of the bank and account details within 30 days of receipt.
key_value: Notice within 30 days; tenant may apply deposit plus 7% interest to rent if noncompliant
coverage_conditions: Landlords who collect security deposits on residential rentals.
exemptions: Seasonal rentals of 125 consecutive days or less; owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings unless the tenant opts in.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Seasonal rental exemption

penalty: Tenant may apply the deposit plus 7% annual interest toward rent
quoted_span:
A landlord or designee who receives security deposit money for ten or less units must 
deposit that money in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an 
interest-bearing account at the current interest rate at the time of deposit.

title: Security deposit return within 30 days
requirement: Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions, by personal delivery or registered or certified mail. The deadline is 5 business days after displacement by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation, and 15 business days after a Safe Housing Act domestic-violence termination.
key_value: 30 days; double damages
coverage_conditions: Residential tenancies subject to the Security Deposit Law.
exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, unless the tenant opts in.
penalty: Double the amount wrongfully withheld plus court costs and attorney fees. Willful withholding from a tenant receiving government assistance carries a civil penalty of $500 to $2,000 per offense.
quoted_span:
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).

title: Law Against Discrimination including source of lawful income
requirement: Landlords may not refuse to rent or discriminate based on a protected class, including source of lawful income. Protected classes include race, creed, sex, familial status, disability, gender identity and sexual orientation.
coverage_conditions: All landlord-tenant relationships.
exemptions: Two-family owner-occupied dwellings; rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home; single-sex residences; age-restricted housing as to familial status.
penalty: Fines up to $10,000 for a first offense (N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a(a)); monetary damages
quoted_span:
The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), 
N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(g) to -(h), prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, 
ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, 
affectional or sexual orientation, gender  identity or expression, mental and physical disability, 
nationality, or source of lawful income.

title: Rent increases may not be unconscionable
requirement: There is no statewide numeric rent cap, but an increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with any municipal rent ordinance. It may take effect only after the old lease is terminated with a valid notice to quit and notice of increase.
key_value: No numeric cap; unconscionability standard
coverage_conditions: Residential tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act.
exemptions: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units (Anti-Eviction Act exception).
quoted_span:
The increase in rent must not be 
unconscionable; it must not be so unreasonable as to shock the conscience of a fair and honest 
person and must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.
conflict_note: Municipal rent control ordinances may impose stricter caps. Under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5, newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. HUD-subsidized and NJHMFA-financed units are not subject to municipal rent control.

title: No rent increases to cover conversion costs
requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, rents may not be raised to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. This applies to all tenants in the building.
coverage_conditions: All tenants in buildings converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee simple ownership.
exemptions: Increases to cover new services or amenities are allowed.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Applies only to buildings undergoing condo/co-op/fee simple conversion

quoted_span:
If a building is converted to a condominium or cooperative form of ownership, or to fee 
simple ownership of units, rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the 
conversion (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31).

title: NJ Law Against Discrimination – source of lawful income protection
requirement: Landlords may not discriminate in housing based on the source of lawful income or the source of lawful rent payment a tenant uses. For example, a landlord cannot deny an apartment to a Section 8 voucher holder based solely on that source of income.
coverage_conditions: Rentals of all real property in New Jersey, residential or business, subject to the LAD's limited exceptions.
exemptions: Rental of one unit in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling. Rental of rooms in a one-family dwelling occupied by the owner or occupant as a residence. Religious-organization preference for persons of the same religion. Familial-status protection does not apply to housing for older persons.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Exempt if a two-family dwelling where the owner occupies the other unit, or a room rental in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling.

penalty: Complaint to the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or to NJ Superior Court within two years of the violation.
citation: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination, N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.
quoted_span:
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses.
conflict_note: Brochure (rev. 2015) does not give the specific section or effective date of the source-of-income provision. The citation is to the LAD generally.

title: FAIR Act: ban on rental property owners using algorithmic rent-setting coordinators
requirement: Rental property owners and their agents may not pay for, subscribe to, contract for, or otherwise exchange consideration for the services of a coordinator (algorithmic revenue management software or device performing a coordinating function). Violations are violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
key_value: Prohibited: paying for or using the services of an algorithmic rent-setting coordinator
coverage_conditions: All rental property owners (any person owning directly or indirectly one or more rental residential dwelling units) and their agents, representatives, or subcontractors, for residential dwelling units used as a primary residence in New Jersey.
exemptions: Excludes government entities setting rents through affordability controls; research/statistical analysis not used to set prices or terms; free public rent estimates; real estate brokerage databases available on equal terms that do not set or recommend prices; spreadsheets without AI requiring human analysis; databases only querying unprocessed data. Excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.
penalty: Violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, P.L.1970, c.73 (C.56:9-1 et seq.); remedies of C.56:9-6 through 9-17 apply. Attorney General complaint portal.
conflict_note: Effective date computed from 'first day of the twelfth month next following the date of enactment' with approval July 20, 2026, yielding 2027-07-01. Section 6(b) prohibits municipalities from enacting ordinances that conflict with this act, which may affect existing local algorithmic rent-setting ordinances (e.g., Hoboken, Jersey City). N.J.S.A. section number inferred from codification range 56:9-20 to 56:9-26.

title: FAIR Act: ban on coordinators performing coordinating functions and on parallel pricing coordination
requirement: No coordinator may facilitate agreements among rental property owners that restrict competition, and no person may perform a coordinating function or engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination using algorithms and competitively sensitive information to set or recommend rents, lease terms, or occupancy levels.
key_value: Prohibited: coordinating function / parallel pricing coordination
coverage_conditions: Any person, coordinator, or agent/subcontractor of a coordinator, including a rental property owner performing a coordinating function for its own benefit, regarding residential dwelling units in New Jersey.
exemptions: Government entities setting or limiting rents through affordability controls; research or statistical analysis not used in setting prices or terms; free public rent estimates; brokerage databases on equal terms that do not set or recommend prices or collect competitively sensitive information for that purpose.
penalty: Violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, P.L.1970, c.73 (C.56:9-1 et seq.); remedies of C.56:9-6 through 9-17 apply.

to residential dwelling units, including by performing a coordinating
function;
conflict_note: Effective date computed as first day of twelfth month following July 20, 2026 enactment (2027-07-01). Section 6(b) bars conflicting municipal ordinances; possible preemption of local algorithmic pricing ordinances. N.J.S.A. section number inferred.

title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protections – just cause required for termination of tenancy
requirement: A landlord may not terminate a tenancy without an enumerated at-fault cause (e.g., nonpayment, material breach, nuisance, criminal activity) or no-fault cause (owner/relative move-in, withdrawal from market, government order, demolition or substantial remodel). The protection applies from the start of the tenancy, and owner move-in for post-6/24/2023 leases requires tenant consent or an express lease clause.
key_value: Just cause required from start of tenancy (>30 days)
coverage_conditions: Residential rental property in the City of San Diego, including mobilehome-park units, for tenancies longer than 30 days. Excludes fixed-term leases of 3 months or less.
exemptions: Hotels/transient occupancy; short-term rentals; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing (Section 8 still covered); mobilehomes under the Mobilehome Residency Law; nonprofit hospitals, religious, care and transitional housing facilities; school dormitories; units where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with a resident landlord; owner-occupied single-family homes renting up to 2 bedrooms/ADUs/JADUs; owner-occupied two-unit structures; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (not mobilehomes); separately alienable units not owned by a REIT, corporation or corporate-member LLC, if the required exemption notice is given.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Exemption for separately alienable units requires a non-corporate/non-REIT owner and a written exemption notice to the tenant (in the lease for tenancies commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01). Owner-occupancy and shared-facility exemptions also apply. Excludes affordable/subsidized deed-restricted housing (except Section 8).

penalty: Tenant civil action for injunctive/equitable relief and damages including punitive damages; wrongful eviction damages of not less than three times actual economic damages; discretionary attorney's fees; affirmative defense in an eviction; noncompliant termination notices are void; City civil and criminal enforcement.
citation: San Diego Mun. Code § 98.0704 (O-21647 N.S., amended O-21769 N.S.)
quoted_span:
A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause. For purposes of this 
Division, just cause includes at-fault just cause and no-fault just cause.
conflict_note: Amended by O-21769 N.S., effective 2024-03-28. The ordinance is stated to be consistent with Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2 and adds protections beyond it.

title: San Diego relocation assistance for no-fault terminations
requirement: For any no-fault just cause termination, the landlord must pay relocation assistance of two months' actual rent, or three months' rent if the tenant is a senior (62+) or disabled. The tenant's income and length of tenancy do not matter. The landlord may pay it directly within 15 days of the notice or waive an equivalent amount of rent.

coverage_conditions: Tenancies in San Diego residential rental property covered by Division 7 that are terminated for no-fault just cause.
exemptions: Same exemptions as SDMC § 98.0703, including housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years. A tenant found at fault for conditions triggering a government vacate order is not entitled to relocation assistance.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Applies only to no-fault terminations. Exemption for separately alienable non-corporate-owned units requires a written exemption notice. Owner-occupancy exemptions apply.

penalty: Landlord liable for not less than three times the required relocation assistance plus actual economic damages; the termination notice is void if § 98.0706 is not strictly complied with.

If the unit is re-offered for rent within five years after an owner move-in, government-order or demolition/remodel eviction, the landlord must first offer it to the displaced tenant, provided the tenant requested this in writing within 30 days of the notice. Landlords must also notify the San Diego Housing Commission of terminations within three business days once its portal is established.

title: San Diego buyout agreement regulations

title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protection Ordinance – just cause for termination
requirement: Landlords may terminate a covered tenancy only for an enumerated at-fault or no-fault just cause. The termination notice must state the cause, and curable lease violations require a prior written notice with an opportunity to cure. Owner move-in under leases entered on or after June 24, 2023 is allowed only with the tenant's written agreement or a lease provision permitting it. Substantial-remodel evictions require posted applications, secured permits and a detailed sworn notice.
key_value: At-fault or no-fault just cause required
coverage_conditions: Tenancies (lawful occupancy over 30 days) in residential rental property in the City of San Diego, including rented dwellings in mobilehome parks. Fixed-term leases of 3 months or less are not covered.
exemptions: Transient hotels; occupancies of 30 days or less; deed- or regulatory-restricted affordable housing and subsidized affordable housing (Section 8 voucher tenants remain covered); MRL mobilehomes; nonprofit hospital, religious, care and transitional housing; school dormitories; units where the tenant shares a kitchen or bath with an owner-occupant; owner-occupied single-family homes renting no more than 2 units or bedrooms; owner-occupied duplexes; separately alienable units not owned by a REIT, corporation or corporate-member LLC, where written exemption notice was given; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes).

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Separately alienable units (e.g., condos, single-family homes) are exempt only if the owner is not a REIT, corporation or LLC with a corporate member AND written exemption notice was given to the tenant. penalty: Tenant may sue for injunctive and equitable relief and money damages, including punitive damages.
